s.en: Along the gallery of the Academy's great lecture hall hung a long row of portraits of past Rectors.
At the head of the row, before the founder's portrait, Sera stopped.
Royal Calendar 300. First Rector, Gregor Wernstein.
White beard. Black coat. Gentle smile.
Every detail was the face of the old man who had smiled down at the students from the stage at assembly that morning.
"They say families resemble one another."
Instructor Regen had appeared beside her without her noticing.
Sera had already confided to him what she'd heard from Viola the night before.
The grey man's words, the Partition Plan, all of it.
"It isn't necessarily mere resemblance. I've long thought so myself."
"According to the Academy's records, each Rector succeeds the moment his predecessor dies. Yet not a single funeral is recorded."
"So he's never once died...?"
"If you kept stealing a hundred years' worth of time from others, it isn't impossible. In theory, at least."
Still looking up at the portrait, he went on in a low voice.
"You're going to meet that grey man, aren't you. I won't stop you. You don't seem the sort who'd listen if I tried."
"But take this with you."
What he held out was a brass disc about the size of a palm.
Fine graduations were cut into its face, and a single needle quivered at its centre.
"A portable recorder. When the flow of time is disturbed nearby, the needle swings."
"It won't tell you whether he's lying, mind."
He smiled, just slightly, with those sleepy eyes.
On the appointed night, a single lamp burned in the canal warehouse.
The wing of the half-built flying machine cast a huge shadow on the wall.
Sera and Viola sat on crates; Niko had his flash tube across his knees and was glaring at the door.
"Just so you know, I still don't trust him."
"Nor do I. But I believe it's worth hearing what he has to say."
Sera held Instructor Regen's recorder tight in her lap.
The needle hadn't moved once.
— and the instant she thought so, it jumped.
"All here, I see."
The voice came from the darkness behind them.
The door hadn't opened. He had stopped time and walked in.
Niko sprang up and levelled the flash tube, but the man, apparently unconcerned, stepped into the circle of lamplight.
"Before we listen, I've got one condition."
Sera stood and looked the man straight in the eye.
"Take off the mask. I won't team up with someone who won't even show his face."
The man said nothing for a while.
Then gloved fingers found the edge of the mask.
The face that emerged from under the grey mask was far younger than she'd expected.
Twenty-five, maybe twenty-six.
An old burn scar ran from his left cheek to his jaw.
His grey eyes were as quiet as an exhausted old man's.
"Reinhardt. ...Or that's what they called me, a hundred years ago."
"A hundred years... Are you the same as the Rector? Have you survived by feeding on other people's time?"
"No. I didn't live through those hundred years. I leapt over them."
Reinhardt sat down on one of the crates.
The lamp flame carved deep shadows in his profile.
"I was born in the year 280 of the Royal Calendar. When the Academy had only just been founded."
"Picked out for my talent in chronomancy, I became an inquisitor answering directly to the Rector. My task was to hunt Rewinders."
The air in the warehouse froze.
"I was taught that Rewinders were heretics who corrupted the order of time. I believed it, and I captured many of them."
"But the real reason was something else. Only Rewinders could undo that man's theft. That's why they had to be wiped out."
"And when did you... realise that?"
"The winter of 302. The night a woman appeared from the far side of time."
Reinhardt drew the silver pocket watch from inside his coat.
On its lid, the same crest as Sera's.
"Elise Milford. She was sheltering the hunted Rewinders, and she stood in my way."
"She could have defeated me. Instead, she spent a night showing me what the Rector was doing."
"The machine at the bottom of the tower, sipping away the city's time. The true face of what I'd been protecting."
Reinhardt's fingers traced the lid of the watch.
"The time-siphon. That's what the Rector called it. Fitted to the crystal's pedestal, it draws up the city's time little by little, and turns it into his own life."
"That's why three seconds disappear every day."
"Then this Partition Plan is..."
"It's no plan to save the city. It's a vessel: stop the lower ring's time, pool it in one place, and drink it all down at once."
"The crystal is failing only because he got too greedy. He means to use that as an excuse to seize the rest in one go."
"...Got the story. But whether I swallow it whole is another matter."
Niko didn't lower the flash tube.
"A hundred years ago you were hunting Rewinders. Now you're telling a surviving Rewinder to lend you a hand. Bit too convenient, no?"
"You're right to doubt me."
Reinhardt didn't argue.
"I captured many, and some never came back. I don't expect forgiveness."
"But — I made a promise to Elise."
"A promise... to my mom?"
"She decided the only way to stop the Rector was to fight him in the era before the time-siphon was installed. So she stayed, a hundred years ago."
"But there are limits to what one can do in a single era. So she made another move. She built the pendulum clock — a gate for crossing time — and sent me forward to this era."
"'In ten years, my daughter's watch will move. When it does, protect her.' That's what she said."
Sera had forgotten even to breathe.
Ten years ago. The night her mother vanished.
"...So ten years on, the watch really did start moving."
"Then just as you came over here, Mom went..."
"The gate lets only one person through at a time. Ten years ago she crossed from this era to a hundred years back, built the gate there, and sent me out."
"I arrived here the same night she vanished. In terms of time, we walked through the same door from opposite sides at the same moment."
Across the far and near sides of time, the story closed into a ring.
"So the date on that plate is the year your mother built the gate in the past."
"Exactly so."
All the while Reinhardt spoke, the recorder's needle stayed still.
Of course, just because the needle was still didn't mean he was telling the truth.
Sera touched the watch in her breast pocket.
Her mother had trusted this man. A man who, a hundred years ago, had been hunting her kind.
"...What do I need to do with my watch?"
"The siphon is protected by a time-loop. Break it, and it rewinds itself to before it broke. A shell of time, repeating the same moment for ever."
"Only a reversing force can break that loop. If you turn time back inside it, the shell collapses under its own weight."
"And does Sera come out of that in one piece?"
Reinhardt didn't answer right away.
His gaze went to the single white strand in Sera's hair.
"...I can't say she'll be unharmed. But it shouldn't cost her life. In theory."
"What d'you mean, 'in theory'!"
"It's fine, Niko."
"If I don't do it, everyone in the lower ring gets stopped, right? Then there's nothing to think about."
"...You're telling me you're not afraid?"
"It's not like I'm not scared. I'm terrified."
"But sitting around doing nothing is scarier."
Viola looked at Sera for a while, then snapped her fan shut.
"Then I shall open the pedestal. If Eisen blood is required, there's no one better suited."
"...Oh, for — fine, fine."
Niko scratched his head roughly.
"On the partition night, the tower'll be sealed top to bottom, right? No getting in the front."
"So we go in from the sky. No other way, is there?"
Every eye turned to the half-built flying machine that filled half the warehouse.
"...That flies?"
"It's not that it won't fly."
"Four days left. I'll make it fly properly."
At that, for the first time, Reinhardt's mouth eased into the faintest of smiles.
The next morning, an unexpected visitor turned up at the warehouse.
Oz, a toolbox slung over his shoulder.
"Grandpa?! How did you know where..."
"I've known where my granddaughter goes for ages."
Oz looked around the warehouse and stopped in front of the flying machine.
He studied the patched-up fuselage with a craftsman's eye.
"...Oi, boy. With joints like these, it'll snap in half up in the sky."
"Eh?"
"Move. I'll do it."
With that, Oz opened his toolbox and set to work without a word.
Niko, still dumbfounded, hurried to start passing him tools.
Early in the afternoon Reinhardt appeared at the warehouse, and Oz's hands stopped dead.
The two men faced each other in silence for a while.
"...So you're the man Elise talked about."
"...She told you?"
"The night before she left. 'Someday someone will come from a long time ago. Trust him.' I thought she was talking nonsense."
Oz snorted and turned back to the flying machine.
"If your hands are free, hold that there. Even a man from a hundred years ago can hold a board."
Reinhardt blinked, thrown for a moment, then silently held the wing board in place.
Viola, watching, gave a small snort of laughter behind her fan.
That night, when Viola got back to the mansion, the lamp was lit in her father's study.
The door stood half open.
"Come in."
She could have run. Instead, Viola pushed the door open.
Her father sat at the desk in the dimmed study, gazing at the globe.
He must have noticed long ago that someone had touched the key under the base.
"I will not ask about the torn page."
"...Father."
"Three nights from now, you will not go near the tower."
He didn't look at her.
"Whatever happens. Understood?"
"Is that an order? Or—"
A request? She couldn't bring herself to say it.
Because her father's back looked so very tired.
He didn't answer.
Viola curtseyed and left the study.
Just before the door closed, she thought she saw her father's lips move, ever so faintly.
I'm sorry.
Perhaps she'd misheard.
But that night, Viola lay awake a long time.
